analysis.one_liner: Protects offshore oil and gas workers from being fired for reporting safety violations or oil-spill risks.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have made it illegal to fire offshore oil and gas workers for reporting unsafe conditions, never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for companies working in offshore oil and gas to fire or punish employees who report safety violations, unsafe conditions, or problems with legally required oil spill response plans. It would set up a complaint process through the Labor Department, offer reinstatement and double back pay to workers who were retaliated against, and require employers to post notices, train workers on their rights, and hand out a card with a hotline number. It was introduced in the final month of the 117th Congress, referred to a committee, and died there without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly the workforce of the offshore oil and gas industry, including contractors and subcontractors: rig and platform workers, spill cleanup and emergency response crews, and job applicants. Today, workers who spot a safety problem or question whether an oil spill response plan is adequate risk their jobs if they speak up. The bill would give them a legal shield, a 180-day window to file a complaint with the Labor Department, a right to a prompt investigation, reinstatement, double back pay, and attorney fees if retaliation is proven.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Offshore oil and gas workers and applicants

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits employers from firing or discriminating against offshore workers who report violations of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, including unsafe conditions and the adequacy of required oil spill response plans [S3].
Protects workers who exercise stop-work authority or refuse a task they reasonably believe could injure them or cause an oil spill [S3].

Establishes a complaint process through the Labor Department with a 180-day filing window, an investigation within 90 days, and preliminary reinstatement orders that take effect even while an employer appeals [S3].
Rewards workers who win: reinstatement, double back pay with interest, expungement of their personnel records, compensatory and exemplary damages, and attorney fees charged to the employer [S3].
Requires employers to post a notice of workers' rights, train employees within 30 days of hiring and yearly after that, and distribute a card with a toll-free Labor Department hotline [S3].
States that the rights cannot be waived by any agreement, including arbitration clauses, and that the bill adds to rather than replaces other worker protections [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas operators, and their contractors and subcontractors, who would bear the cost of investigations, reinstatement and double back pay when retaliation is found, compensatory and exemplary damages, attorney fees, and the administrative work of posting notices and running annual training. More broadly, companies would lose the practical ability to sideline workers whose reports about safety or spill plans threaten production schedules or regulatory standing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore oil and gas operators and contractors

drawbacks.text: Employers would face significant new liability: double back pay, exemplary damages, attorney fees, and a preliminary reinstatement order that takes effect before the appeal is decided, which some would argue is a heavy remedy for a contested firing [S3].

The 'reasonably believes' standard lets a worker trigger protection based on a subjective belief, and the bill covers contractors, subcontractors, grantees, and consultants, which employers would say invites disputes and compliance costs across a web of companies [S3].
The Labor Department would need to stand up a new intake, investigation, and adjudication process for this industry within 30 days of enactment, adding administrative burden [S3].
The bill is narrow: it covers only offshore oil and gas workers, so the same retaliation problem for workers in onshore energy or other offshore industries would remain unaddressed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is worker safety versus employer control. When a rig worker reports an unsafe condition or questions a spill response plan, the public has a direct interest in that report getting out — the consequences of silence in offshore drilling include worker deaths and catastrophic spills. The bill's remedies are aggressive by design, because a fired whistleblower with only ordinary back pay has little reason to complain. The main honest criticisms are the breadth of the liability and the administrative lift, not the principle. As a one-industry bill introduced with almost no cosponsors in the last weeks of a Congress, it was never realistically going anywhere, but its design follows the model of existing sector-specific whistleblower laws.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and never came up again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark DeSaulnier (D-CA) introduced the Offshore Oil and Gas Worker Whistleblower Protection Act on December 2, 2022, in the final month of the 117th Congress [S1].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor, which is the first step for most labor bills, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The bill had only one cosponsor, a House Democrat [S4].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the committee or the full House ever voting on the bill [S1].

The bill's purpose was to close a gap in protections for offshore oil and gas workers, who had no equivalent of the retaliation shields other safety laws give workers when they report violations, unsafe conditions, or inadequate oil spill response plans [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas operators are better off: no retaliation liability, no mandatory training and hotline costs, and no workers empowered to press stop-work and spill-plan concerns with legal backing. Offshore workers who witness unsafe conditions remain exposed if they speak up.

for.name: Rep. Mark DeSaulnier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on December 2, 2022

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat in the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for markup or reported it out during the final month of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were House Democrats; no Republican supported it and the committee, then run by Democrats, also took no action, so the bill never had a visible bipartisan base.

industries.industry: Offshore oil and gas operators and their contractors
industries.note: The bill would have made it illegal to fire or punish workers who report safety violations, unsafe conditions, or inadequate spill response plans, and imposed training, notice, and hotline duties. The industry's practical interest — keeping production moving and quieting reports that could trigger regulators — runs against the safety reporting the bill protects, and the consequences of unprotected reporting fall on workers and coastal communities alike.

These workers would gain a retaliation shield, a complaint process, reinstatement with double back pay, and attorney fees. Their interest in reporting a hazard is the same as the public's interest in hearing about it.
